introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.
enonce_intro_markdown: A particle $P$ moves on the curve with polar equation $r = e^{\sqrt3\,\theta}$, where $(r, \theta)$ are polar coordinates relative to a fixed pole $O$.
incertitudes: Question 5 : l'exposant imprimé (scan) se lit « e puissance racine de 3 fois theta » (r = e^(sqrt(3) theta)) ; cette lecture est confirmée par (ii), qui donne tan(psi) = 1/sqrt(3), soit pi/6, comme le sujet l'annonce. Pour (ii) on suppose que P se déplace dans le sens des theta croissants (theta' > 0) ; si le sens est inverse, le vecteur vitesse est simplement inversé et la droite OP fait toujours un angle de pi/6 avec la tangente.

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the radial component of the acceleration of $P$, leaving your answer in terms of $r$, $\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}\right)^2$ and $\dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}$. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radial component of the acceleration in polar coordinates is $\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2$.

Since $r = e^{\sqrt3\,\theta}$, we have $\dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = \sqrt3\,r$. By the chain rule

$$\dot r = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\dot\theta = \sqrt3\,r\dot\theta.$$

Differentiating again with respect to $t$ (product rule, and $\dot r = \sqrt3\,r\dot\theta$ once more):

$$\ddot r = \sqrt3\left(\dot r\dot\theta + r\ddot\theta\right) = \sqrt3\left(\sqrt3\,r\dot\theta^2 + r\ddot\theta\right) = 3r\dot\theta^2 + \sqrt3\,r\ddot\theta.$$

Radial component:

$$a_r = \ddot r - r\dot\theta^2 = 3r\dot\theta^2 + \sqrt3\,r\ddot\theta - r\dot\theta^2 = 2r\dot\theta^2 + \sqrt3\,r\ddot\theta.$$

$$\boxed{a_r = 2r\left(\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right)^2 + \sqrt3\,r\,\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Deduce that $OP$ always makes an angle $\dfrac\pi6$ with the velocity of $P$. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity has a radial component $v_r = \dot r$ (along $OP$) and a transverse component $v_\theta = r\dot\theta$ (perpendicular to $OP$). From part (i), $\dot r = \sqrt3\,r\dot\theta$.

Let $\psi$ be the angle between the velocity and $OP$. Then, taking $\dot\theta > 0$,

$$\tan\psi = \frac{v_\theta}{v_r} = \frac{r\dot\theta}{\sqrt3\,r\dot\theta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}.$$

This value does not depend on $r$, $\theta$ or $t$. Since $0 < \psi < \dfrac\pi2$ (both components are positive), $\psi = \dfrac\pi6$ at every instant.

$$\boxed{\psi = \frac\pi6\ \text{always}}$$

(This is the property of the equiangular spiral $r = e^{\theta\cot\alpha}$: here $\cot\alpha = \sqrt3$, so $\alpha = \dfrac\pi6$.)
